terms.d: Points better than an average test side on a neutral ground: +10 means a side expected to beat an average test team by ten. Built from every result, with home advantage, travel and rest taken out.
The rating's two halves: points a side scores above an average side, and points it keeps out.
How often we think a side wins a match like this one. 70% still loses 3 times in 10.
Rugby draws are rare (about 2 in 100 tests): we give the chance the final margin lands on zero.
The points we expect the favourite to win by, on average. Half of tests land within about eight points of it.
The points we expect both sides to score together.
World Rugby's points-exchange rankings, rebuilt by us from results with the published formula. From 28 September 2026 our table starts from the published points and adds every result since.
What a result moves in the World Rugby rankings: the winner takes points from the loser, more for beating a stronger side, half as much again for winning by more than 15, double at a World Cup.
A try bonus point for scoring four or more tries; a losing bonus point for losing by seven or fewer. The Six Nations adds three for a Grand Slam.
Winning all five Six Nations matches.
A Home Nation (England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales) beating the other three in one Six Nations.
Finishing last in the Six Nations.
A rate per 80 minutes on the pitch (a full test). Minutes come from the substitutions.

Our player value: points added per 80 minutes above a replacement-level player in the same position, from what each carry, break, tackle, turnover and penalty is worth to the scoreboard (a model fitted on past tests), plus goal kicking above an average kicker.
The 20th percentile of the position among regular test players: the level a side can always find on the bench.
Where a player ranks among regular test players in the same position group: 90th means better than 90 in 100.
Front row (props and hookers), locks, back row (flankers and number 8s), half-backs (scrum-halves and fly-halves), centres, back three (wings and full-backs).
A team stat shifted by how much its opponents usually allow: 400 metres against a side that concedes 500 is less than 400 against one that concedes 300.
The line across the pitch where a phase starts: a carry over it is going forwards.
A carry that goes through the defensive line.
Tackles made out of tackles attempted (made plus missed).
Appearances in the matches our source carries. Older and smaller tests are missing, so this is not a player's official cap count.
Whether our chances mean what they say: of the tests we gave 70%, about 70% should have gone that way.
Scores for a forecast against what happened; lower is better. A coin flip on a two-way result scores 0.693 log loss and 0.25 Brier (rugby's rare draws make ours three-way).

Tier one: the Six Nations and Rugby Championship sides. Tier two: the other regular World Cup sides (Fiji, Japan, Georgia, Samoa, Tonga, the Americas' and Iberia's leading sides and others). Tier three: everyone else. We use tiers for a new side's starting rating and to say where our forecasts have been tested.
We choose every setting on 2004-2018 and score once on 2019 onwards, so the published accuracy is honest.
